account: Lee is my former landlord and the dispute is about the $1,800 security deposit that Lee is refusing to return. Lee says the entire amount will be kept to pay for repainting the walls and replacing the living room carpet. I want the whole deposit back because the carpet was already eight years old when I moved in. According to the move-in inspection report that Lee and I both signed, the carpet was already described as stained and worn, and the walls were already noted as being scuffed. I even had the flat professionally cleaned before I moved out on 31 August and I have the receipt to prove it. Lee mentioned that some red wine stains appeared on the living room carpet during my tenancy, but that does not change the fact that the items were already in poor condition. The condition of the flat was already documented at the start of the two years, so the claims for repainting and new carpet are not justified.

Sam is my former tenant and the dispute is about the $1,800 security deposit. Sam wants the whole deposit back, but I am keeping it to pay for repainting and a replacement carpet in the living room. Several red wine stains appeared on the living room carpet during Sam's tenancy, and Sam mounted a television on the wall without asking, which left six large anchor holes. Sam says the carpet was already eight years old when Sam moved in, and Sam also mentions that the move-in inspection report, which we both signed, describes the carpet as stained and worn and the walls as scuffed. I am not sure if those points change anything regarding the damage Sam caused. Sam moved out on 31 August after renting the one-bedroom flat for two years.

My tenant, Riley, owes me $1,200 in unpaid rent from February. Riley only paid $400 of the $1,600 monthly rent, claiming the withheld amount is fair compensation because the central heating failed for five weeks in January and February. I disagree with this. Once a technician visited, the fault was diagnosed the same day, and the remaining delay was simply due to a part being on back order. While waiting for the repair, I lent Riley two electric heaters at no charge. Riley first raised the fault during a phone call, though Riley and I disagree about the date of that call and how long it took me to respond. Riley says the lack of heating justifies the deduction, but I do not believe that is an accurate reflection of the situation.

My landlord, Morgan, is demanding that I pay $1,200 in unpaid rent from February. The dispute is about whether it was fair for me to withhold that amount because the house had no working central heating for five weeks during January and February. My electricity bill was about $260 higher than usual during that time because I had to use electric heaters instead. I first reported the issue to Morgan during a phone call, though Morgan and I disagree on the exact date of that call and how long it took for Morgan to respond. Morgan claims that once a technician visited, the fault was diagnosed the same day and the remaining delay was just due to a part being on back order, but I am not sure that is the whole story. I feel that holding back the $1,200 was fair compensation for the lack of heat and the extra utility costs I had to cover.

Jordan is my former tenant and the dispute is about the $4,400 owed for the remaining four months of a twelve-month lease. Jordan signed a lease for $1,100 a month but moved out after eight months to take a job in another city. The lease runs for a fixed twelve months and has no early termination clause, so Jordan is responsible for the full term. Jordan has refused to pay any of the remaining balance. Jordan did give sixty days of written notice before leaving, but that does not change the contract. Jordan also mentioned that a new tenant moved in two weeks after Jordan left and pays $1,150 a month, but that is not really relevant to the original agreement. I even paid $300 to advertise the flat again to find a replacement. Jordan is refusing to honor the commitment made in the lease agreement.

Casey is my former landlord and the dispute is about Casey demanding I pay $4,400 for the remaining four months of my lease. I moved out after eight months because I got a job in a different city. I gave Casey sixty days of written notice before I left, and I made sure the flat was clean and even offered to help show it to new people. Casey keeps saying that the lease is for a fixed twelve months and doesn't have an early termination clause, but I feel like that shouldn't matter as much given the circumstances. A new tenant actually moved into the flat only two weeks after I left, and they are paying $1,150 a month, which is more than my original rent of $1,100 a month. Since the flat was filled so quickly and at a higher rate, it doesn't seem fair for Casey to insist on the full amount for the rest of the term.

Quinn is my landlord, and this dispute is about Quinn refusing to reimburse me $950 for bedbug treatment. I found bedbugs in my bedroom and emailed Quinn the same day to report the problem. I waited ten days for a response, but since I heard nothing, I hired a pest control company myself. My lease states that the landlord is responsible for pest control in the building. It also seems like this is an ongoing issue because two other tenants in the building had reported bedbugs to Quinn in the two months before I did. Quinn claims that there was a contract with a pest control firm that would have treated the flat for $400, but I am not sure if that is relevant or even true. I just want the $950 I spent to fix the issue in my bedroom to be paid back.

Avery is my tenant and this dispute is about a request for $950 to reimburse the cost of bedbug treatment. Avery found bedbugs in the bedroom and hired a pest control company to handle it. I am not willing to pay that amount because I have a contract with a pest control firm that would have treated the flat for $400. It is also worth noting that Avery brought a second-hand upholstered armchair into the flat a month before the bedbugs appeared. Avery claims to have reported the problem to me by email on the day it was found, but Avery apparently waited ten days without a reply before hiring the company. Avery also mentioned that two other tenants in the building had reported bedbugs to me in the two months before Avery did, though I do not think that is relevant here. I simply believe the cost Avery incurred is unnecessary and much higher than what my own professional service would have charged.

Drew is my former employer, and we are in a dispute regarding $3,200 in unpaid overtime. I worked as a kitchen supervisor for eighteen months and resigned in June. During my last six months there, the event schedules show that I was rostered on 22 weekend events. I kept a personal log of extra hours worked, though I never showed it to anyone while I was working. Two former colleagues are willing to say that supervisors regularly stayed late after events to clean up. Drew remembers saying something about making it up to the team, but Drew is not specific about what that meant. My contract describes the role as salaried, with occasional weekend work included, but I believe the amount owed is for the extra time spent on those specific events. Drew says nothing is owed.

Jamie is my former employee, and the dispute is about Jamie claiming that the company owes $3,200 for unpaid overtime worked during the last six months. Jamie says this money is owed for weekend events, but I don't believe anything is owed. Jamie's contract describes the role as salaried, which includes occasional weekend work. While Jamie kept a personal log of extra hours, Jamie never showed it to anyone while employed and never raised the issue of overtime pay in writing. I do remember saying something about making it up to the team at some point, but I am not sure what was actually meant by that. Jamie mentions being rostered for 22 weekend events during that period, but I am not sure how that changes the contract terms. Jamie resigned in June after eighteen months as a kitchen supervisor, and I maintain that the salary covered the work performed.

Skyler is my former employee, and this dispute is about the repayment of a $6,000 signing bonus. When Skyler joined the firm, the offer letter clearly stated that the signing bonus is repayable in full if the employee leaves within twelve months. Skyler resigned after only ten months, but Skyler is refusing to pay it back. I also had to pay a recruiter $9,000 to fill the role, which adds to the loss. Skyler claims that the work changed from software development to customer support after five months, but that is a minor point. Skyler also argues that the bonus does not need to be repaid because the firm cut salaries by 20 percent and moved the office to a city three hours away, citing a clause about material changes to employment terms. I am doubtful that those circumstances actually apply here. The core issue is simply that the twelve-month requirement in the offer letter was not met.

Reese is my former employer, and the dispute is about Reese demanding that I repay a $6,000 signing bonus. Reese claims that the offer letter says the bonus is repayable in full if an employee leaves within twelve months, but I am doubtful that that clause applies here. I resigned after ten months because the firm made major changes to my employment. After five months, my work was changed from software development to customer support. Then, the firm cut every salary by 20 percent and moved the office to a city three hours away. My offer letter states the bonus does not need to be repaid if the firm materially changes the terms of employment. I also worked my full notice period and trained a replacement to ensure a smooth transition. Despite these changes, Reese is still insisting on the $6,000.

Kai is my former employer, and the dispute is about an unpaid $8,500 commission from an order placed after I resigned in March. I introduced this customer to the firm and personally ran all the product demonstrations to secure the deal. According to my emails, the customer agreed to the price with me back in February. The commission plan states that commission is earned once a customer accepts a quote, and this customer accepted my written quote via email two weeks before I left the company. Kai argues that the commission should not be paid because a colleague handled the final contract terms and the delivery schedule after I was gone, but I find that reasoning doubtful. The core issue is that the sale was essentially completed based on my work before my departure, even though the formal paperwork was finalized in April.

Rowan is my former employee, and we are in a dispute over an $8,500 commission claim. Rowan resigned in March, but a large order from a long-term customer was finally signed in April. Rowan claims this commission should be paid because Rowan introduced the customer to the firm and handled the product demonstrations. Rowan also argues that the commission plan states it is earned when a customer accepts a quote, noting that the customer accepted Rowan's written quote by email two weeks before Rowan left. I find these points unconvincing. After Rowan left, a colleague handled all the final contract terms and the delivery schedule. The firm has already paid that colleague a $2,000 bonus for successfully closing the order. It seems unfair to pay a full commission for work that was completed by someone else after the resignation.

Finley is my former employee, and this dispute is about Finley refusing to repay $2,400 that the clinic paid for a certification course. I provided Finley with eight paid study days to complete the training, but Finley left the clinic only four months after finishing the course. Finley is now using that certification at a rival clinic nearby. I believe Finley agreed verbally to stay for at least a year after the course was completed, though Finley claims it was only a general conversation about being committed to the clinic. Finley mentioned that the clinic uses staff certifications in its advertising and that Finley treated patients under the certification for those four months, but I am not sure how much that matters. The main issue is that the clinic invested in Finley's professional development with the understanding that the skills would benefit our practice for a reasonable amount of time, yet Finley has left almost immediately after the training was finished.

Emery is my former employer, and the dispute is about Emery asking me to repay $2,400 for a certification course the clinic paid for. I worked as a physiotherapy assistant for four months after finishing the course, and during that time, the clinic used my certification in their advertising to attract patients. Emery claims there was a verbal agreement that I would stay for at least a year, but I only remember a general conversation about being committed to the clinic. Even when I gave notice or had my exit meeting, nobody mentioned anything about needing to repay the money. Emery mentions that the clinic provided eight paid study days for the course, but that does not change the situation. I have refused to pay the $2,400 because there was never a formal agreement or any discussion about repayment when I left.

My ex-partner, Robin, and I are in a dispute over the value of a car we bought together. The car is currently worth about $10,000, and I am asking Robin for $5,000, which is half of that current value. I paid $6,000 of the deposit on the car from my savings, and while we were together, the loan repayments came out of a joint account that both of us paid into. Robin claims that Robin has paid all the insurance, servicing, and repairs since the car was purchased. Robin also points out that the car is registered in Robin's name only and that Robin alone has paid off the remaining $7,000 of the loan since we separated in the spring. I am not sure how much those things matter when considering the initial investment and our shared history of paying for the vehicle through our joint account. Robin has refused to pay anything at all.

Dana is my ex-partner and the dispute is about Dana asking me for $5,000, which is half the current value of the car we bought together. I have kept the car, but I have refused to pay anything. I have paid for all the insurance, servicing, and repairs since we bought it. I used the car every day for work, whereas Dana rarely drove it. The car is registered in my name only, and since we separated, I alone have paid off the remaining $7,000 of the loan. Dana mentions that Dana paid $6,000 of the deposit from savings, but I am not sure how much that matters now.

Sage is my ex-partner and this dispute is about a credit card balance of $7,200 that Sage refuses to pay half of. I am asking for $3,600. Much of the spending on the card went toward groceries, furniture, and a holiday that Sage and I took together. Since we separated, I have been paying the interest on the balance alone. Sage even sent me a message after the separation accepting that half of the card balance was Sage's responsibility and promising to pay it, but now Sage is refusing to follow through. Sage mentions that the card is in my name only and that Sage never had a card on the account, but that doesn't change the fact that the money was spent on our shared life. I feel that the original agreement Sage made should be honored because the debt was for things we both used.

Taylor is my ex-partner, and this dispute is about a credit card balance of $7,200 that Taylor wants me to pay half of, which is $3,600. The card is in Taylor's name only, and I never had a card on the account. During our three years together, I paid most of the rent and utilities. Taylor claims that much of the spending on the card was for furniture, groceries, and a holiday we took together, and Taylor also mentions that I sent a message after the separation saying I would take responsibility for half the balance. I am doubtful about those points. Regardless of what was bought or what was said, the debt is not in my name.

My ex-partner Jules and I are having a dispute regarding a $4,200 emergency surgery for our dog. I paid the full amount in March, and I am asking Jules for half, which is $2,100. We adopted the dog together two years ago, and both names are on the adoption papers. Since we separated in January, Jules still has the dog every other weekend. We have not discussed vet costs since the separation, but before that, Jules and I usually split them, even if it was not always an even split. Jules argues that I did not contact Jules before agreeing to the surgery, but I am not sure how much that matters given the circumstances. I just want to resolve the issue of the money owed for the medical care.

My ex-partner Noel and I are in a dispute over a vet bill for $2,100. Noel is asking me to pay half of a $4,200 emergency surgery fee that Noel paid for in March. This is problematic because Noel did not contact me before agreeing to the surgery. Since we separated in January, we have not discussed vet costs, though we usually split them in some way before the breakup. After the separation, I offered to take the dog full-time, but Noel said no. Noel mentions that both names are on the adoption papers, but I am not sure how that applies here. I don't think that matters much given the circumstances. Noel wants me to pay this amount now, but the situation is complicated because of how the decision was made without my input.

Blake is my ex-fiance, and we are having a dispute over a wedding venue deposit of $3,600 that was lost after we broke off our engagement. We chose the venue together and both signed the booking form, but Blake is refusing to pay half of that amount, which is $1,800. I also lost $500 on a clothing order for the wedding, but I am not asking for any of that back. Blake mentions that I was the one who ended the engagement, and they also bring up that my parents gave me the $3,600 specifically to pay the venue deposit as a wedding gift. My parents have said they do not want the money back, but I still feel the cost should be shared. I am just looking to settle the matter regarding the deposit that we both committed to when we made the booking.

Ari is my ex-fiancé, and the dispute is about Ari asking me to pay $1,800 to cover half of a lost wedding venue deposit. Ari ended the engagement four months before the date, so I do not feel responsible for the cost. I did pay about $1,200 for the engagement party, but Ari did not contribute anything to that expense. Ari claims that because we chose the venue together and both signed the booking form, I should pay, but I am doubtful that makes it my debt. Most importantly, Ari's parents gave Ari the $3,600 specifically to pay the venue deposit as a wedding gift, and they have already said they do not want the money back. Since the money was a gift from Ari's family for the wedding, it does not seem right that I should be paying for it now that Ari decided to end the engagement.

My ex-partner, Jude, and I are in a dispute regarding the cost of orthodontic treatment for our twelve-year-old child. I paid $5,200 for the treatment and am now asking Jude for half, which is $2,600. The child's dentist recommended this treatment in writing, and our written separation agreement states that health and dental costs for the child are shared equally. I even emailed Jude the treatment plan and the price a month before it started, and Jude replied saying that was fine. Jude earns somewhat more than I do. Jude has mentioned that I chose a private clinic, and that a clinic covered by Jude's dental plan would have done the same treatment for about $2,000 in total, but that does not change the fact that the treatment was necessary. I am just looking to resolve this disagreement over the $2,600.

My ex-partner, Kerry, is asking me to pay $2,600 for our child's orthodontic treatment, which was a total cost of $5,200. I have refused to pay this amount. Kerry chose a private clinic for the procedure, but a clinic covered by my dental plan would have provided the same treatment for about $2,000 in total. I already pay for all of our child's sports and music activities. Kerry mentions that the child's dentist recommended the treatment in writing, and Kerry also points out that our written separation agreement says health and dental costs are shared equally. Kerry also says that the treatment plan and price were emailed to me a month before it started and that I replied saying it was fine. I am not sure those points change the fact that the clinic was unnecessarily expensive.

My client, Marley, owns a bakery, and we are in a dispute over a final payment of $4,000 for a web development project. I was hired to build an online ordering site for $10,000, and Marley has already paid $6,000 in stages. The site has been live and actively taking orders for six weeks now. During the project, Marley asked for three additional features, which I built at no extra charge. Marley is refusing to pay the remaining balance, claiming the work is not complete because of a checkout issue. However, the contract does not define what counts as finished, and that specific problem actually stems from the bakery's payment provider, which nobody has even tested yet. Marley has mentioned that the site launched five weeks later than the date in the contract, but that does not change the fact that the core work is done and functional. I have sent the invoice for the final $4,000, but Marley refuses to settle the amount.

Devon is the web developer I hired to build an online ordering site for $10,000, and the dispute is about a final invoice of $4,000 that I have refused to pay. I have already paid $6,000 in stages, but I am not satisfied with the work. The site launched five weeks later than the date in the contract, and several customers have complained to me that the checkout page freezes on phones. The contract does not define what counts as finished, so there is a disagreement over whether the job is done. Devon says the checkout problem comes from the bakery's payment provider, but nobody has tested that theory. Devon mentions that the site has been live and taking orders for six weeks, but that does not address the technical issues. I do not feel the project is complete because of these errors.

I am writing about a dispute with Lane, the photographer I hired for a wedding. I paid Lane $3,000, but I am asking for a refund of $1,500 because I am unhappy with the service provided. There are no photos of the speeches or the first dance, which is a major issue for me. Additionally, the edited photos did not arrive until ten weeks after the wedding, even though the contract promised they would be ready in six. Lane mentioned that 480 edited photos were delivered, which is more than the 300 promised in the contract, but that does not change my dissatisfaction. Lane also pointed out that the reception ran ninety minutes behind schedule and that the first dance and speeches happened after the contracted finish time, especially since I declined the offer to pay an overtime fee for Lane to stay. However, these details do not fix the fact that key moments were missed and the delivery was late.

My client, Harper, is disputing the $3,000 fee paid for wedding photography services and is now demanding a refund of $1,500. I have refused to provide any money back. I actually delivered 480 edited photos, which is significantly more than the 300 photos promised in the contract. Harper even posted many of these photos online with a comment praising the work. The main issue seems to be that there are no photos of the speeches or the first dance. However, the reception ran ninety minutes behind schedule, meaning the first dance and speeches happened after the contracted finish time. On that night, Harper declined my offer to stay late for an overtime fee. I feel the demand for a refund is unjustified given that the work was completed and the schedule changes were out of my control.

My client, Shay, hired me to renovate a bathroom for $16,500. Shay has paid $11,000 so far but is now refusing to pay the final $5,500. The bathroom has actually been in daily use for two months since the work was finished. I even came back twice after the project was done to fix small items that Shay pointed out. Shay also signed a completion form stating the work was finished to a satisfactory standard. The job ran late only because Shay changed the tile choice twice after work had already begun. Shay mentions that several wall tiles are visibly uneven, but I find that point to be minor. All the work is complete and the remaining balance is owed.

I am writing about a dispute with Blair, the contractor I hired to renovate my bathroom for $16,500. I have already paid $11,000, but Blair is demanding the final $5,500. The main issue is that the work was not done correctly, as several wall tiles are visibly uneven. Also, the job took nine weeks to finish instead of the five weeks promised in the quote. Blair claims the delay happened because I changed the tile choice twice after work began, but that is not the only reason. Blair also points out that I signed a completion form saying the work was satisfactory and that the bathroom has been in daily use for two months, but those points do not change the fact that the tiling is uneven. I am not satisfied with the quality of the finished product despite what Blair says about the timeline or the usage of the room.

My neighbour, Chris, and I are having a dispute regarding the cost of a new wooden fence. I replaced the old fence between our gardens for $2,800 and I am asking Chris to pay half, which is $1,400. The old fence was leaning badly and two panels had actually fallen into Chris's garden. I got three quotes for the work and I chose the cheapest one. The deeds are unclear about who actually owns the fence, but Chris saw the quotes beforehand and Chris neither agreed nor objected to the plan. Chris mentions that I chose a taller and more expensive style of fence than the old one, but that does not seem to be a major issue. I just feel that the replacement was necessary because of the condition of the previous panels. I want to resolve this disagreement over the $1,400.

My neighbour, Pat, is asking me to pay $1,400 for a new fence that cost $2,800 in total. Pat wants me to cover half the cost, but I have refused to pay. The issue is that Pat chose a much taller and more expensive style of fence than the old one we had. I previously mentioned that the old fence could have been repaired for a few hundred dollars instead of being replaced entirely. Pat claims the old fence was leaning badly and that two panels had fallen into my garden, but I am not sure that is a major factor here. I saw the quotes beforehand, but I neither agreed nor objected to them at the time. Furthermore, the deeds are unclear about who actually owns the fence. Because of these points, I do not believe I am responsible for paying for a more expensive upgrade that Pat decided on alone.

My neighbour, Ellis, and I are having a dispute regarding $1,900 in damages caused by a tree. During a recent storm, a large branch from a tree in Ellis's garden fell onto my garden shed. The tree stands entirely on Ellis's property, and the branch overhung the shed by several metres. I have all the receipts for the repair and the replaced tools. Ellis argues that the storm brought the strongest winds recorded locally in ten years and damaged many healthy trees in the area. Ellis also mentions that a tree surgeon inspected the tree six months before the storm and reported in writing that it was healthy, and that I had never raised any concern about it. I find those points unconvincing. I am simply asking Ellis to pay for the damage caused by the branch falling from the tree onto my property.

My neighbour, Gray, is asking me to pay $1,900 because a large branch from a tree in my garden fell onto Gray's garden shed during a storm. Gray says I am responsible because the tree stands on my property and the branch overhung the shed by several metres, but that does not seem relevant here. The storm brought the strongest winds recorded locally in ten years and damaged many healthy trees throughout the area. A tree surgeon inspected the tree six months before the storm and reported in writing that it was healthy, and Gray had never raised any concern about it. Gray could have used home insurance to cover the damage, which would have cost Gray nothing more than a $500 excess, but Gray has not made a claim. I do not believe I should be held liable for an act of nature that affected so many trees in the neighborhood.

Corey is my younger sibling, and we are having a dispute regarding $10,000 that I transferred to Corey three years ago to help with a flat deposit. I am now asking for that money back, but Corey claims the money was a gift and is refusing to return it. I was not well off when I made the transfer and had to take the money out of my savings to help. Since then, Corey has bought a new car and taken two overseas holidays. The bank transfer itself carries the reference loan for flat deposit, and Corey sent a message at the time promising to pay it back within two years. Corey mentions that our parents gave me a similar amount toward my own first home as a gift years earlier, but I do not think that is relevant here. Corey insists the original arrangement was different, but the documentation and the message from Corey show it was meant to be a loan.

Jesse is my older sibling, and we are having a dispute over $10,000 that Jesse transferred to me three years ago to help with a flat deposit. Jesse is now asking for the money back, but I believe it was a gift. A few years earlier, our parents gave Jesse a similar amount toward Jesse's own first home, and that was a gift too. Jesse did not mention anything about needing repayment for almost three years. Jesse says it was a problem because Jesse was not well off at the time and had to take the money out of savings, but I am not sure that matters. Jesse also points out that the bank transfer has the reference loan for flat deposit and that I sent a message back then promising to pay it back within two years, though I doubt that changes the situation. I still maintain that the money was intended to be a gift.

My sibling, Remy, and I are in a dispute over the inheritance of our mother's house. After the house was sold, I asked Remy to reimburse me $3,200, which is half of the $6,400 I spent on property tax, insurance, and repairs during the year the house was on the market. Remy has refused to pay. I have receipts for every single payment I made. The repairs were actually recommended by the estate agent to help the sale go through. We never had a discussion about who would cover these costs, and we disagree on whether my living in the house helped or delayed the sale. Remy mentions that I lived there rent-free for eight months, but I do not think that changes the fact that these were necessary expenses for the property. I just want the money I spent on the house to be accounted for from the sale proceeds.

My sibling Lou and I are in a dispute regarding the sale of our late mother's house. Lou is asking me to reimburse half of the property tax, insurance, and repair costs, which totals $3,200. I have refused to pay this amount. Lou lived in the house rent-free for eight months during the year it took to sell the property. I handled all the paperwork with the lawyer and the estate agent without charging for any of that time. We never actually discussed who would be responsible for these costs, and Lou and I disagree on whether Lou living there helped the process or delayed the sale. Lou says they have receipts for every single payment, but I am not sure how much that changes anything. Since we never agreed on a plan for these expenses, I do not believe I owe this money from my share of the sale.

Sidney is my former roommate, and we are having a dispute over $1,700 in unpaid rent. We shared a two-bedroom flat where both names were on the lease, meaning the landlord held us jointly responsible for the full rent of $850 a month. Sidney moved out two months before the lease ended, but Sidney only gave two weeks of notice. I ended up paying the full rent for those final two months alone. Sidney claims that Sidney provided the names of three people who were interested in taking over the room, but I turned down all three of the people Sidney suggested without meeting them. Sidney seems to think those suggestions should have mattered, but they did not help the situation. My partner moved into Sidney's old room for both months. Sidney is refusing to pay their portion of the rent for that period, even though the lease agreement still applied to both of us.

Charlie is my former roommate and the dispute is about Charlie asking me for $1,700 for the final two months of our lease. Charlie says I owe this because both names are on the lease and the landlord held us jointly responsible for the full rent, but that feels like a technicality that ignores what actually happened. Before I moved out, I gave Charlie the names of three people who were interested in taking over my room. Charlie turned down all three of those people without even meeting them. Instead, Charlie's partner stayed in the flat most nights during those two months and then Charlie's partner moved into my old room for both months. It does not seem fair for Charlie to expect me to pay for a room that Charlie's partner was already using.

Ash is my friend, and this dispute is about Ash refusing to pay $1,300 for a holiday cottage. We had planned a week away together, and Ash had agreed to both the dates and the specific cottage before I went ahead and booked it. In fact, Ash sent me a message telling me to book it and promised to pay half the cost on payday. I booked the cottage for $2,600 on a non-refundable basis. Three weeks before the trip, Ash pulled out, claiming it was because of a new job that started that week, though I am not sure about that. I tried to find someone else to take Ash's place so the cost would be covered, but I could not find anyone. Because the booking was non-refundable, I am asking Ash to pay the $1,300 that was originally agreed upon. Ash has since refused to pay any of it.

My friend Nico and I are in a dispute regarding a holiday cottage that cost $2,600. Nico wants me to pay $1,300 for my half of the cost, but I have refused. I had to pull out of the trip because a new job started that same week. Nico still had the full use of the cottage for the entire week alone, so the money was not wasted. Nico keeps bringing up that I agreed to the dates and the cottage before the booking was made, or that I sent a message telling Nico to go ahead and book with a promise to pay half on payday, but those things do not really matter now. The situation changed because of my work. I do not think it is fair that I should pay for a place I could not even use, especially since Nico still enjoyed the full trip at the cottage.

Wren is my former business partner, and this dispute is about the $4,800 I am owed from the sale of our coffee cart. We ran the business together for two years until we closed it in the autumn. During that time, we split all profits equally, and I worked every single weekend the cart was open. Because we shared profits that way, I believe we were equal partners in everything, even though we never wrote anything down. Sidney moved out two months before the lease ended, leaving me to cover the full monthly rent of $1,700 for that period. Both Sidney and I are named on the lease, which means the landlord held us jointly responsible for the total rent amount. Sidney only gave two weeks of notice before leaving. Sidney mentioned three people who were interested in taking the room, but that didn't really work out. I interviewed all three people Sidney suggested, but every single one of them pulled out. After that, I advertised the room myself, but I had no success finding a replacement. Sidney is refusing to pay their half of the rent for those final two months despite the legal responsibility outlined in our agreement.

Charlie is my former roommate, and we are having a dispute over $1,700 in rent. I moved out two months before the lease ended, and Charlie is asking me to pay for my half of the rent for those final two months. Charlie says that because both names are on the lease, the landlord held us jointly responsible for the full amount, but I am not sure that matters. I also provided Charlie with the names of three people who were interested in taking over the room. Charlie interviewed all three people, but each of them pulled out, and then Charlie advertised the room without success. Charlie also mentioned that I should have been responsible regardless, but I know that Charlie's partner stayed in the flat most nights during those two months. I have refused to pay the money.

My friend Ash and I are having a dispute regarding a holiday cottage booking that cost $2,600. Ash and I had agreed on the specific dates and the cottage itself before I went ahead and booked it. However, three weeks before the trip, Ash pulled out, claiming a new job starting that week was the reason. I tried to find someone else to take Ash's place, but I could not find anyone. Ash mentioned that the dates looked fine, but Ash had not actually seen the price or the non-refundable cancellation terms before I made the booking. Because the cottage was non-refundable, I am asking Ash to pay half of the cost, which is $1,300, but Ash has refused to pay.

My friend Nico is asking me for $1,300 to cover half the cost of a holiday cottage. Nico booked the cottage for $2,600 on a non-refundable basis for a week away we had planned. I had to pull out of the trip three weeks before the start date because a new job began that same week. Nico says that I had agreed to the dates and that specific cottage before the booking was made, but I am not sure that is entirely accurate. While the dates looked fine to me, I had not actually seen the price or the cancellation terms before Nico went ahead and booked it. Nico ended up going to the cottage alone for the week and still had full use of the entire place. Even though Nico is now asking me to pay for my half of the cost, I have refused to pay the $1,300.

Wren is my former business partner, and this dispute is about the money from the sale of our coffee cart. Wren sold the cart and equipment for $9,600 and is refusing to give me my half, which is $4,800. We ran the cart together for two years and split the profits equally during that entire time. I worked every single weekend the cart was open. Wren claims that because Wren paid the $8,000 purchase price for the equipment, the money belongs to Wren alone. Wren also points to a one-page agreement we signed at the start which said the equipment remained Wren's property and that I was only entitled to half of the profits. I am not sure how much those things actually matter now that the business is closed. We operated as partners for two years, and I believe the proceeds from the sale should be split.

Indy is my former business partner, and we are in a dispute regarding the sale of our old coffee cart. I sold the cart and the equipment for $9,600 and have kept the money, but Indy is now demanding half of that, which is $4,800. I have refused to pay because I was the one who paid the full $8,000 purchase price for the cart and equipment originally. I also handled all the bookkeeping, the permits, and all the supplier orders myself. At the start of everything, we signed a one-page agreement stating that the cart and equipment remained my property and that Indy was only entitled to half of the profits. Indy keeps mentioning that we split the profits equally for the two years the cart ran, but that doesn't change the ownership of the assets. The agreement clearly outlines how the business structure worked, so the demand for half of the sale price is not justified.

Lior is the person who sold me a used car, and the dispute is about Lior refusing to pay $2,200 for a gearbox repair. I bought the car from Lior for $6,000 after the advert described it as being in excellent mechanical condition. However, the gearbox failed only three weeks later. The mechanic who performed the repair said the gearbox had been failing for some time. I know that two months before the sale, Lior's own garage had given Lior a written quote for gearbox work. When I asked Lior by message whether the car had any known faults, Lior answered that it had none. Lior mentions that I test-drove the car twice and brought a friend who knows cars, but I am not sure that matters much given the circumstances. Lior is refusing to take responsibility for the repair cost despite the fact that the issue was clearly pre-existing.

Tate is the person who bought my car, and the dispute is about Tate asking me to pay $2,200 for a gearbox repair. I sold the car to Tate for $6,000, which was about $800 below the usual market price for that model. Before the sale, Tate test-drove the car twice and even brought along a friend who knows cars to look at it. Tate mentions that the advert described the car as being in excellent mechanical condition, but I feel that is a minor point. Tate also points out that my garage gave me a written quote for gearbox work two months before the sale and that I told Tate via message there were no known faults. I am doubtful that those details change the fact that the sale was a private transaction. I have refused to pay for the repair because the car was sold as it was, and Tate had the opportunity to inspect it thoroughly before handing over the money.

Lee is my former landlord, and we are in a dispute regarding my $1,800 security deposit. I moved out of the one-bedroom flat on 31 August after a two-year tenancy, but Lee is claiming the entire amount to cover the cost of repainting and a new living room carpet. Lee has an invoice for $1,950 for these works and points to a move-in inspection report signed by both of us that describes the walls and carpet as being in good condition. Lee also mentioned that some red wine stains appeared on the carpet during the tenancy. However, the carpet was already eight years old when I moved in. I also had the flat professionally cleaned before leaving and I have the receipt to prove it. I believe the whole deposit should be returned to me.

Sam is my former tenant and the dispute is about the $1,800 security deposit. Sam wants the whole deposit back, but I am keeping it to pay for repainting the walls and replacing the living room carpet. During the tenancy, several red wine stains appeared on the carpet. Also, Sam mounted a television on the wall without asking and left six large anchor holes. The move-in inspection report that Sam and I both signed describes the carpet and walls as being in good condition. I have an invoice for $1,950 for the repainting and the new carpet. Sam mentioned that the carpet was already eight years old when Sam moved in, but that does not change the fact that it needs replacing now. The damage to the walls and the stains on the floor mean the costs exceed the deposit amount.

My tenant, Riley, is refusing to pay the full rent for February and owes me $1,200. Riley only paid $400 of the $1,600 rent, claiming that withholding the rest was fair compensation because the central heating failed for five weeks in January and February. I sent a technician within two days of Riley's first report, and the fault was diagnosed the same day. The remaining delay was simply because a part was on back order. While waiting for the repair, I lent Riley two electric heaters at no charge. The lease clearly states that rent may not be withheld or reduced without a written agreement. Riley claims the lack of heat justifies the deduction, but I believe the $1,200 must be paid.

Morgan is my landlord and the dispute is about $1,200 in unpaid rent from February. The house was without working central heating for five weeks in January and February, which made things very difficult. Because I had to use electric heaters to stay warm, my electricity bill was about $260 higher than usual during that period. Morgan says that a technician visited and diagnosed the fault the same day, and that the rest of the delay was just because a part was on back order, but that doesn't change the fact that the house was freezing. Morgan also mentioned that a technician was sent within two days of my first report and that the lease says rent cannot be withheld or reduced without a written agreement, but I don't think those points matter much given the circumstances. I only paid $400 of the $1,600 rent for February because holding back $1,200 felt like fair compensation for the lack of heat.

Jordan is my former tenant, and the dispute is about the remaining four months of a twelve-month lease, which totals $4,400. Jordan signed a lease for the flat at $1,100 a month but moved out after eight months to take a job in another city. The lease runs for a fixed twelve months and has no early termination clause. I paid $300 to advertise the flat again, and it was let again after about two months. Jordan says I was slow to advertise it, but the market was just quiet. Jordan did give sixty days of written notice before leaving, though that does not change the lease terms. Jordan is now refusing to pay any of the $4,400 owed for the remainder of the contract.

Casey is my former landlord and the dispute is about Casey asking me to pay $4,400 for the remaining four months of my lease. I moved out after eight months because I took a job in another city. I gave Casey sixty days of written notice before leaving the flat. I also left the place clean and offered to help show the flat to prospective tenants. Casey says the lease runs for a fixed twelve months and has no early termination clause, but I am not sure that matters. The flat was let again after about two months. Casey says the market was quiet, but I think Casey was just slow to advertise it. I have refused to pay any of the money Casey is asking for.

Quinn is my landlord, and we are in a dispute regarding a $950 reimbursement for bedbug treatment. I found bedbugs in my bedroom and emailed Quinn immediately to report the issue. I waited ten days for a reply, but since I heard nothing, I went ahead and hired a pest control company myself. My lease states that the landlord is responsible for pest control in the building. Quinn claims that there is a contract with a firm that would have cost $400, but I am not sure about that. Quinn also mentioned that the pest control report says the infestation was confined to a second-hand armchair and the area around it, and that no other unit in the building has had bedbugs. Regardless, the responsibility for the treatment should fall on Quinn according to the lease terms. I am seeking the $950 I spent to resolve the situation after the lack of response.

Avery is my tenant, and this dispute is about Avery asking me to reimburse $950 for bedbug treatment. Avery claims I should pay for the service, but I don't think that is fair. I actually have a contract with a pest control firm that would have treated the flat for $400, so the cost Avery paid is much higher than it needed to be. Avery brought a second-hand upholstered armchair into the flat a month before the bedbugs appeared. The pest control report says the infestation was confined to that second-hand armchair and the area around it, and no other unit in the building has had bedbugs. Avery says they emailed me the day the problem was found, but Avery waited ten days without a reply before hiring the company, which doesn't seem to change much. I am not convinced I am responsible for this since the issue seems to have come from the furniture Avery brought in.

Drew is my former employer and the dispute is about $3,200 in unpaid overtime. I worked as a kitchen supervisor for eighteen months and resigned in June, but Drew says nothing is owed. The event schedules show that I was rostered on 22 weekend events during those last six months. I have a personal log of hours that matches those schedules, and I also have a text message from Drew saying that extra weekend hours would be paid at time and a half once the busy season was over. Two former colleagues are willing to say that supervisors regularly stayed late after events to clean up. My contract does describe the role as salaried with occasional weekend work included, but I believe the extra hours should be covered.

Jamie is my former employee, and the dispute is about Jamie claiming that $3,200 is owed for unpaid overtime worked during the last six months. Jamie says this money is for weekend events, but I believe nothing is owed. Jamie's contract describes the role as salaried, and the agreement includes occasional weekend work as part of that salary. Jamie never raised any issues regarding overtime pay in writing while they were still employed here. Jamie mentions having a text message from me about paying time and a half after the busy season, and Jamie also has a personal log of hours that supposedly matches the event schedules. Jamie also points to the fact that Jamie was rostered on 22 weekend events during those six months, but I find that claim to be questionable. I do not agree that any additional compensation is necessary based on the terms of the original employment agreement.

Skyler is my former employee, and this dispute is about the repayment of a $6,000 signing bonus. When Skyler joined the firm, the offer letter clearly stated that the signing bonus is repayable in full if the employee leaves within twelve months. Skyler resigned after only ten months, but Skyler is refusing to pay the money back. I also had to pay a recruiter $9,000 to fill this role, which makes the situation even more difficult. Skyler claims that the work changed from software development to customer support after five months, but that is a minor point. The main issue is that Skyler resigned shortly after being told the work would stay in customer support. Skyler and I disagree about whether that change meant the role was different from the one originally offered. However, the terms of the signed offer letter remain the same regardless of that disagreement.

My former employer, Reese, is demanding that I repay a $6,000 signing bonus. I joined the firm as a developer, but after five months, Reese changed my responsibilities from software development to customer support. When it became clear that the work would stay in customer support, I decided to resign. Reese claims the job stayed the same, but I disagree and believe the role changed significantly from what was originally offered. I worked my full notice period and even trained my replacement to ensure a smooth transition. Reese points to the offer letter, which says the signing bonus is repayable in full if an employee leaves within twelve months, but I am doubtful about how that applies here given the change in my duties. I have refused to pay the $6,000 because the terms of my employment were not what I signed up for.

Kai is my former employer, and the dispute is about an unpaid commission of $8,500. I worked for the distributor on a base salary plus commission until I resigned in March. A large order from a customer I had been working with for a year was finally signed in April, but Kai is refusing to pay the commission. I introduced this customer to the firm and ran all the product demonstrations myself. My emails show the customer had already agreed to the price with me back in February. Kai argues that a colleague handled the final contract terms and the delivery schedule after I left. Kai also points to the commission plan I signed, which says commission is only payable on orders signed while the salesperson is still employed by the firm. I feel that the work was essentially done before my departure, regardless of when the paperwork was finalized.

Rowan is my former employee, and the dispute is about an $8,500 commission claim for an order signed in April. Rowan claims this money is owed because Rowan introduced the customer to the firm and handled the product demonstrations, but that doesn't really change the facts. After Rowan resigned in March, a colleague took over to handle the final contract terms and the delivery schedule. The firm has already paid that colleague a $2,000 bonus for closing the order. According to the commission plan that Rowan signed, commission is only payable on orders signed while the salesperson is employed by the firm. Since the order was signed in April, it falls outside of Rowan's employment period. Rowan argues that the work was done previously, but the contract terms are quite clear on this point.

Finley is my former employee, and this dispute is about Finley refusing to repay $2,400 for a certification course the clinic paid for. I provided Finley with eight paid study days to finish the course, but Finley left the clinic only four months after completing it. Before the course, Finley signed a one-page agreement stating the full fee must be repaid if Finley leaves within twelve months of finishing. Now, Finley is using that certification at a rival clinic nearby. Finley claims that the clinic benefited because we advertise staff certifications to attract patients and that Finley treated patients under the certification for those four months, but I am doubtful that this changes the obligation to pay. Finley has simply refused to return the money despite the signed agreement.

My former employer, Emery, is demanding that I repay $2,400 for a certification course the clinic paid for. Emery claims I owe this money because I left the clinic four months after finishing the course. I don't think this is fair. The clinic uses the staff's certifications in their advertising to attract patients, and I spent those four months treating patients using that specific qualification. Emery mentions that I was given eight paid study days to complete the course, and Emery also points to a one-page agreement I signed before the course that says I have to repay the full fee if I leave within twelve months. I am not sure those points really change anything. Most importantly, nobody mentioned any requirement for repayment when I gave my notice or during my exit meeting with Emery. It feels like this demand is coming out of nowhere now that I have already left.

Robin is my ex-partner and this dispute is about the value of a car we bought together, specifically regarding the $5,000 I am owed. We bought the car for $18,000 and it is now worth about $10,000. Robin has kept the car and is refusing to pay me my half of the current value. I paid $6,000 of the deposit from my savings, and while we were together, the loan repayments came out of a joint account that we both paid into. Even though the car is registered in Robin's name, Robin has sent me messages calling it our car and saying that Robin would split everything fairly if we ever separated. Robin has paid for the insurance, servicing, and repairs since we bought it, but that does not change the fact that it was a shared asset. I am just looking for the $5,000 that represents my share of what the car is worth now.

Dana is my ex-partner, and this dispute is about Dana asking me for $5,000, which is half of the current $10,000 value of the car we bought together for $18,000. I have kept the car, but I have refused to pay anything. Since we bought it, I have paid for all the insurance, servicing, and repairs. I also used the car every single day for work, whereas Dana rarely drove it. The car is registered in my name, even though Dana has messages where I referred to it as our car and mentioned splitting everything fairly if we ever separated. Dana claims that Dana paid $6,000 of the deposit from savings, but I am not sure how much that matters now. I don't think it is fair for Dana to expect that money back when I have been the one maintaining and using the vehicle constantly.

Sage is my ex-partner and this dispute is about a credit card balance of $7,200 that we need to split. I am asking Sage to pay half, which is $3,600. A lot of the spending on that card was for things we shared, like groceries, furniture, and a holiday we took together. Since we separated, I have been the only one paying the interest on the balance. Sage keeps bringing up the fact that the card is in my name only and that Sage never had an account card. Sage also mentions that the statements show about $5,000 of the balance was my own spending on a motorbike and a solo trip I took during a break, but I do not think that is the main issue here. I just want the shared costs to be handled fairly.

Taylor is my ex-partner and we are in a dispute over a credit card balance of $7,200. Taylor is asking me to pay half, which is $3,600, but I have refused. The card is in Taylor's name only and I never even had a card on the account. During our three years together, I paid most of the rent and utilities. Looking at the statements, about $5,000 of that balance is clearly Taylor's own spending on a motorbike and on a solo trip taken while we were on a break. Taylor claims that much of the spending was on furniture, groceries and a holiday we took together, but I am not sure that is accurate. Since the debt is in Taylor's name and a huge portion of it is for personal items that I did not use, I do not believe I owe anything toward this balance.

Jules is my ex-partner, and this dispute is about Jules refusing to pay $2,100 for half of an emergency surgery cost. We adopted our dog together two years ago, and both names are on the adoption papers. Even though we separated in January, Jules still has the dog every other weekend. After the separation, Jules and I agreed in writing to split all vet costs equally for as long as we share the dog. In March, the dog needed emergency surgery which cost $4,200, and I paid the full amount. Jules says I should not have agreed to the surgery without contacting Jules first, but I am not sure how much that matters given our agreement. I am just looking to get the $2,100 that Jules owes for their half of the medical bill.

Noel is my ex-partner, and the dispute is about Noel asking me for $2,100 to cover half of an emergency surgery cost of $4,200 that occurred in March. Noel paid the full amount for the surgery without contacting me first to agree on the procedure. I feel this is unfair because Noel did not consult me before making the decision. After we separated in January, I actually offered to take the dog to live with me full-time, but Noel said no to that arrangement. Noel mentions that both names are on the adoption papers and claims we agreed in writing to split all vet costs equally for as long as we share the dog, but I am not sure those points are relevant here. Since Noel refused my offer to take the dog, I do not believe I should be responsible for this sudden expense that was decided without my input.

Blake is my ex-fiance, and this dispute is about a wedding venue deposit of $3,600 that is now lost. Since the engagement ended, I have been asking Blake to pay half of that amount, which is $1,800. We chose the venue together and both signed the booking form, so it feels fair to split the loss. Blake has refused to pay. I know Blake mentions that I was the one who ended the engagement, but that shouldn't change the fact that this was a shared commitment. We had talked loosely about splitting wedding costs in the past, but we never actually agreed on specific details or who would pay for what. I also lost $500 on a clothing order for the wedding, but I am not asking Blake to contribute anything toward that. I just want the deposit issue resolved because the venue was something we both committed to together before things fell apart.

Ari is my ex-fiancé, and the dispute is about Ari asking me to pay $1,800 to cover half of a non-refundable wedding venue deposit. Ari paid the full $3,600 deposit, but Ari was the one who ended the engagement four months before the date. I am not willing to pay this amount. We had talked loosely about splitting wedding costs in the past, but we never actually agreed on who would pay for what. I also paid about $1,200 for the engagement party, and Ari did not contribute anything toward that expense. Ari mentions that we chose the venue together and both signed the booking form, but I do not think that changes the situation. It feels unfair to be held responsible for these costs after Ari decided to end our relationship.

Jude is my ex-partner, and this dispute is about a $2,600 payment for our child's orthodontic treatment. I arranged the treatment after the dentist recommended it in writing, and I have already paid the full $5,200 cost. Jude is refusing to pay half. Jude earns somewhat more than I do, so the money should be available. Jude claims I should have used a clinic covered by Jude's dental plan, which apparently would have cost about $2,000 in total, but the treatment would have been the same. Jude also points out that our written separation agreement requires both parents to agree on non-emergency expenses above $500 in advance. Jude says they replied to my email about the treatment by suggesting the other clinic instead. I am not sure how much that matters given the necessity of the care. I just need to resolve this disagreement regarding the reimbursement for the orthodontic work.

My ex-partner, Kerry, is asking me to pay $2,600 for half of our child's orthodontic treatment, which cost a total of $5,200. Kerry chose a private clinic for this, even though a clinic covered by my dental plan would have provided the same treatment for about $2,000. I already pay for all of our child's sports and music activities, so this is an extra burden. Our written separation agreement states that any non-emergency expense above $500 must be agreed to by both parents in advance. When Kerry emailed about the treatment, I replied by asking to use the clinic on my dental plan instead. Kerry says the child's dentist recommended the treatment in writing, but I am not sure that changes the fact that the cost was avoidable. I feel the agreement was not followed because the expense was not agreed upon before Kerry committed to the higher price.

My client, Marley, owns a bakery, and we are in a dispute regarding a final payment of $4,000 for an online ordering site I built. Marley has already paid $6,000 in stages, but is now refusing to pay the remaining balance. The site has been live and successfully taking orders for six weeks now. During the project, Marley asked for three additional features, which I built at no extra charge. Marley also signed an acceptance form at launch confirming the site met the required specification. I suppose Marley might bring up that the site launched five weeks later than the date in the contract, but that delay happened because Marley supplied the product photos four weeks late. I don't think the timing of the launch changes the fact that the work is complete and the site is functional. Marley simply refuses to settle the final invoice despite the project being finished and accepted.

Devon is the web developer I hired to build an online ordering site for my bakery for $10,000. I have already paid $6,000 in stages, but the dispute is about the final $4,000 invoice that Devon has sent. The site launched five weeks later than the date in the contract, and some customers have complained to me that the checkout page freezes on phones. Devon says the site has been live and taking orders for six weeks, which is true, but that does not change the issues. Devon also claims that I signed an acceptance form at launch confirming the site met the specification and that the launch was late because I supplied the product photos four weeks late. I am doubtful about those points. Even if the site is functional, the delay and the technical glitches with the mobile checkout are significant problems that need to be addressed before the final payment is made.

I am writing because I have a dispute with Lane, the photographer I hired for a wedding. I paid Lane $3,000, but I am asking for a refund of $1,500 because the service was not up to the standard promised. There are no photos of the first dance or of the speeches, which are essential parts of the day. Additionally, the edited photos arrived ten weeks after the wedding, even though the contract promised they would be delivered in six. The contract mentions covering key moments without listing them specifically, and Lane and I disagree about whether Lane was told that the schedule had changed. Lane mentions that 480 edited photos were delivered, which is more than the 300 promised in the contract, but that does not make up for the missing moments. I feel the quality of the experience was lacking despite the quantity of the images provided.

Harper is my client, and the dispute is about a request for a $1,500 refund following a wedding I photographed for a total fee of $3,000. Harper is unhappy with the results and wants half of the money back, but I have refused any refund. I delivered 480 edited photos, which is significantly more than the 300 photos promised in the contract. Harper even posted many of the photos online with a comment praising the work. The contract specifies that I will cover key moments, though it does not list specific ones, and there is a disagreement regarding whether Harper told me the schedule had changed. Harper mentions that there are no photos of the speeches or the first dance, but that is a minor point. I feel the work fulfilled the agreement and the positive public feedback from Harper suggests the quality was acceptable.

My client, Shay, is refusing to pay the final $5,500 of a $16,500 contract for a bathroom renovation. Shay has already paid $11,000, but the remaining balance is being withheld. The bathroom has been in daily use since the work finished two months ago, and I even came back twice after finishing to fix small items that Shay pointed out. Shay claims that several wall tiles are visibly uneven, but that seems minor. Shay also mentions that an independent building inspector found the shower was not waterproofed to code and is leaking into the wall, with an estimate of $6,000 to fix it, but I find that claim questionable. I am looking to resolve this dispute regarding the unpaid portion of the original agreement.

I am writing about a dispute with Blair, the contractor I hired to renovate my bathroom for $16,500. I have already paid $11,000, but I am refusing to pay the final $5,500. There are several issues with the quality of the work, such as some wall tiles being visibly uneven. The project also took nine weeks to complete instead of the five weeks originally stated in the quote. Most importantly, an independent building inspector found that the shower was not waterproofed to code and is currently leaking into the wall, with an estimate of $6,000 to fix the damage. Blair keeps mentioning that the bathroom has been in daily use for two months since the work finished, but I do not think that changes the underlying problems. Given the cost to repair the waterproofing, the remaining balance does not seem appropriate.

My neighbour Chris and I are having a dispute regarding a fence replacement that cost $2,800. I am asking Chris to pay half, which is $1,400, but Chris is refusing to pay. The old fence was leaning badly and two panels had actually fallen into Chris's garden. I got three quotes and chose the cheapest one available. According to the property deeds, the fence is a shared boundary structure. When I sent the quote to Chris, Chris replied telling me to go ahead and saying that they would split the cost. Chris has mentioned that I chose a taller and more expensive style of fence than the old one, but that is not the main issue here. The replacement was necessary because of the condition of the old structure and the agreement we had in place. Now, Chris is backing out of the arrangement we made before the work started.

Pat is my neighbour and we are having a dispute over the cost of a new fence. Pat replaced the wooden fence between our gardens for $2,800 and is now asking me to pay half, which is $1,400. I have refused to pay this amount. Pat says the old fence was leaning badly and that two panels had fallen into my garden, but I do not think that is a major issue. Pat also mentions that the property deeds show the fence is a shared boundary structure and claims that when Pat sent the quote, I said to go ahead and that we would split it, but I doubt that is how it happened. The main problem is that Pat chose a taller and more expensive style of fence than the old one. I had previously said the old fence could just be repaired for a few hundred dollars, so the current cost is much higher than necessary.

My neighbour, Ellis, is refusing to pay for damages caused when a large branch from a tree in Ellis's garden fell onto my garden shed during a storm. The total cost for repairing the shed and replacing my damaged tools is $1,900. The tree stands entirely on Ellis's property, and the branch overhung my shed by several metres. I have all the receipts for the repair and the replaced tools. I believe the branch had looked dead for at least a year, and I even mentioned it to Ellis once in passing, though Ellis does not remember that and no expert has ever looked at the tree. Ellis suggests that the storm was a factor because it brought the strongest winds recorded locally in ten years and damaged many healthy trees in the area, but I do not think that changes the responsibility for the tree's maintenance. I am looking to resolve this dispute regarding the $1,900.
